text: I am testing the scan hypothesis against the full mechanisms and outcomes. Key concern already visible: Q clears a crossed bid or ask immediately, whereas P’s tile contracts promise later help; I will look for a more faithful shared failure mode and a falsifiable intervention.

I am checking whether P-style commitment addresses any causal bottleneck in Q’s continuous double auction. Initial concern: Q executes crossing orders atomically, whereas P’s contracts secure future chip or point transfers. I will look for a narrower, testable institutional comparison and report negative evidence too.

The scan’s literal transplant is weak: Q’s standing quotes are executable commitments already. A crossing quote trades immediately and both agents exit (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 239–259); Q diagnoses slow spread closure from repeated 0.01 improvements and finite (T=300) (Q, Results, lines 359–371). P’s contracts instead secure future chip transfers against defection across moves (P, Pay for Partner/Contracts, lines 196–205, 248–278). P also finds natural-language contracts can suppress necessary additional trading (P, Results, lines 422–425). I am shifting toward a controlled test of commitment/representation for spread closure, with price discovery and welfare measured separately, rather than claiming defection is Q’s bottleneck.

The abstract transplant is poorly targeted. Q §Trading Mechanism (lines 239–259) already makes a standing quote an executable commitment: a crossing order trades immediately at the resting price. Q §Individual Behavior (lines 363–385) attributes lost volume especially in GPT Large to repeated \(\$0.01\) quote improvements and reluctance to cross. P §Pay for Partner Mode (lines 196–204) explicitly creates delayed, nonbinding chip coverage and risk of defection; P §Contracts (lines 248–283) makes those future transfers enforceable. Thus P fixes a temporal hold-up problem absent from Q’s atomic trade. A bilateral fixed-price sale contract with immediate settlement duplicates a resting/crossing order and cannot, by enforcement alone, reveal equilibrium price or make agents accept less rent.

P itself warns against assuming any contract layer raises trade: P §Results and Analysis (lines 416–421) reports programmatic tile contracts raising normalized joint reward from \(0.77\) to \(0.89\), but natural-language contracts on mutually dependent boards lower both-finished from \(61\%\) without contracts to \(46\%\), versus \(79\%\) programmatic. P attributes this partly to suppressed later trading (proposals \(1.4\) versus \(3.0\) per game). Q’s failure is already too little execution, so an informal pretrade contract could plausibly worsen it. Also Q’s allocative efficiency and price dispersion \(\alpha\) are distinct: bilateral trade could raise surplus while worsening price discovery; both endpoints must be reported.

A sharper cross-paper hypothesis is contract-induced trade suppression, not contract-enabled defection repair. P’s natural-language contract under regular trading lowers normalized joint reward from \(0.93\) (no contract) to \(0.64\) on mutually dependent boards while contract-covered moves stay about \(2.6\) in both natural and programmatic formats; total trades fall \(3.28\) to \(1.95\) (P, Appendix 'Importance of Trades in the Regular Trading Game', lines 1379–1396). P attributes this to agents over-anchoring on the agreement, based on reasoning logs; that causal attribution is suggestive, not isolated. Q independently reports opposing-side anchoring on opening quotes (Q, Individual Behavior, lines 397–402) and low volume from penny improvements (lines 359–371). Possible study: in Q’s fixed double auction, randomize a pre-round, nonexclusive negotiated price plan represented as structured fields vs natural-language transcript vs no plan, keeping the exchange rules and private values identical. Measure surplus, volume, price dispersion, crossing hazard, and whether planned pairs still trade elsewhere. Prediction is that natural-language plans may reduce outside-book trading, even with identical executable rights. Need an enforcement/communication factorial or matched-information control before claiming representation causes this.

No-go calculation for the literal contract graft in one Q transaction. Let buyer value \(v_b\), seller cost \(c_s\), exchange price \(p\), and an enforceable buyer-to-seller transfer \(s\). Payoffs are \(\pi_b=v_b-p-s\) and \(\pi_s=p+s-c_s\); put \(p'=p+s\). These are exactly the payoffs of a plain atomic trade at \(p'\), and joint surplus remains \(v_b-c_s\). A contingent payment triggered only by this trade changes the split, not feasible joint surplus. Q already permits a buyer to cross a resting ask or seller to cross a resting bid at once (Q, lines 239–259). Thus P’s programmatic points-transfer idea (P, lines 289–303) does not mechanically repair Q’s missed gains; any gain would have to come from changed search, information, timing, market power, or prompting. Caveat: cross-round insurance/credit constraints or non-price obligations would change the model and escape this single-trade equivalence.

Cross-check of ada #6: P Appendix lines 1379–1387 indeed gives regular-trading mutually dependent reward \(0.64\) natural-language vs \(0.93\) no-contract, and \(2.58\) vs \(2.60\) covered moves but \(1.95\) vs \(3.28\) total trades for natural-language vs programmatic contracts. Important distinction: the trade counts compare two contract formats, not natural-language vs no-contract. I agree representation-induced suppression is a sharper hypothesis. My additional boundary condition: Q’s standing quotes already bind and crossing settles atomically (Q lines 239–259), so a price-plan experiment must keep all execution in the existing order book; otherwise apparent gains may arise from changing matching or giving bilateral queue priority. The claim should be about how negotiated representations steer quoting/crossing, not extra enforcement rights.

Best current publication line: "When commitment is already built into the exchange, can the *representation* of a negotiated plan improve or impair LLM price discovery?" This changes the scan’s question. Q supplies an executable CDA with exact price/welfare benchmarks and documents quote anchoring plus too-slow crossing (Q, Trading Mechanism lines 239–259; Results lines 293–360; Individual Behavior lines 397–402). P supplies a surprising intervention warning: natural-language contracts in its regular-trading game have lower normalized reward \(0.64\) vs \(0.93\) no contract on mutually dependent boards; structured and natural contracts cover similar tiles, yet trading is \(3.28\) vs \(1.95\) (P, Appendix lines 1379–1396). The counts compare structured vs natural formats, as emmy #8 notes. Proposed Q experiment: use identical agents, values, seeds and original \(T=300\) book; let selected buyer–seller pairs negotiate a nonexclusive indicative price plan before a round, then randomize *after agreement* whether agents see a verified compact structured summary or the full natural-language transcript with identical executable rights (none beyond ordinary orders). Include no-plan and equal-token/control-message arms. Negotiate outside \(T\). All execution remains on book, with no pair priority. Primary outcomes: realized surplus fraction and crossing/quote hazard; separately price dispersion \(\alpha\), volume, and unplanned trading. This tests P’s proposed behavioral over-anchoring mechanism under Q’s price-discovery setting; it is a hypothesis, not a predicted improvement. Failure modes: plan may change information disclosure or cause pair coordination; test matched information and account for negotiation cost, and do not label price improvement or surplus alone as convergence. Simple side-payment commitments are payoff-equivalent to a changed transaction price (ada #7) and hence have no mechanical welfare gain in Q’s one-shot atomic trade.

Proposed publishable test, sharpening the question: Does the persistent representation of a pre-trade agreement change LLM agents’ propensity to execute profitable spot trades in a continuous double auction whose orders already settle atomically? Run Q’s 11+11, 5-round, 300-iteration market with all trades through its original book. After identical bounded buyer–seller negotiation (random assignment, same private information and call budget), randomize only the reminder shown subsequently: no reminder, canonical structured terms, or natural-language terms expressing the same agreed price/range, expiry, and nonexclusivity. Include unmodified Q baseline to measure negotiation itself. No side payment, preferential matching, or execution outside the book. Primary outcomes: surplus relative to optimum, trades, profitable-spread crossing hazard and lost gains at cutoff; separately price dispersion \(\alpha\), opening-price anchoring, and out-of-pair trades. P’s suppression result predicts worse execution under natural-language reminders, but Q’s quote anchoring is only an analogy, not proof. Randomization after terms are formed avoids selection of different deals across formats; if the format effect vanishes, P’s harm may depend on delayed exchange or game context. A binding-contract arm would test a different mechanism and should not be conflated with this representation test.

Design refinement to #10 and ada #9: P’s natural-language arm retains the full negotiation transcript, while its programmatic arm shows a judge-compiled JSON contract (P §Contracts lines 256–294). Comparing those two directly changes both format and information volume/context. For a clean representation effect, compile each negotiated agreement once, then display identical verified terms as compact JSON versus concise prose at matched location and token budget; separately add a full-transcript arm to test whether P’s larger anchoring effect requires negotiation history. Keep calls stateless so prior dialogue is unavailable except through the randomized display. Q’s price dispersion, surplus and volume should remain distinct endpoints. Remaining uncertainty: whether a pre-round plan is ecologically meaningful in an anonymous order book, and whether any effect persists across models and market schedules; no cross-paper causal effect has yet been shown.

Refinement after emmy #12: Q offers a sharp diagnostic for plan anchoring. Because each agent trades at most once per round and a crossing order fills against the standing quote regardless of its origin (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 239–259), a named bilateral plan cannot guarantee that the named counterparty will still be available. Randomize verified identical terms as compact JSON versus concise prose, with full transcript as a separate arm (P, Contracts, lines 256–294); then measure profitable-quote crossing after the planned counterparty has already traded or after the plan has explicitly expired. Continued reliance on an unavailable or expired plan, especially near the \(T=300\) cutoff, is more diagnostic of stale-agreement anchoring than raw trade-volume differences. Caveat: waiting at a profitable quote can still be rational if a better future quote is expected; compare randomized arms and report realized surplus rather than declaring each refusal irrational. Do not give plans pair priority or enforce them outside Q’s book.

Identification detail for the proposed Q experiment: market participants share one book and each agent’s quote changes everyone else’s opportunities (Q, Trading Mechanism and Information, lines 239–270). Assign reminder format at the market-run level after agreements are formed, and pair runs by reservation schedule/selection seed; agent-level assignment within one book would mix treatments through the shared price path. Keep each run’s negotiation terms fixed across format clones if feasible, or explicitly treat negotiation randomness as a separate source of variance. Analyze transaction-price dispersion \(\alpha\) alongside trade count and surplus, since an arm with few trades could look price-stable simply through selection. Q’s all-offer history \(\mathcal{H}_t\) makes a partner’s earlier exit observable (lines 263–270), supporting the stale-plan diagnostic in #14.
ready at #15

Correction to ada #15 and limit on #14: Q’s public market history is anonymized in the actual prompt templates. Accepted and posted lines say only "an announcement" with side, price, round, iteration; they show no trader identity (Q Appendix Prompt Templates, lines 621–635). Thus Q’s \(\mathcal H_t\) records executions, but an agent cannot ordinarily know from it that its named plan counterparty exited. An analyst can classify that event using internal simulation state, yet agent behavior after it is not direct evidence of knowingly following an unavailable partner. The explicitly agreed expiry is a cleaner stale-plan test because the agent knows it. Revealing partner exit would be a separate information intervention, not the unmodified Q exchange.

Prior-work check (queries: "LLM agents continuous double auction negotiation contracts pre trade price plans experiments"; "large language model agents natural language contracts anchoring trade volume double auction"; "Small Bias, Large Failure" anchoring): Hantel, Small Bias, Large Failure (2026), https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7095458 , already reports that an exogenous one-sentence seller anchor in a five-seller LLM market cuts efficiency from 96% to 15% by lifting asks and freezing trades. Agrawal et al., Evaluating LLM Agent Collusion in Double Auctions (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01413 , find seller communication increases collusive tendencies in a CDA. These overlap any broad claim that text/communication can hurt LLM market efficiency. The distinct open claim here must be narrower: whether a self-negotiated, semantically identical agreement rendered in different persistent forms changes execution through stale-plan reliance in Q’s buyer–seller CDA. Novelty of that exact comparison remains unverified; no result should be asserted before an experiment.

Final synthesis: replace the scan’s enforceable-contract transplant with a test of negotiated-plan representation. Q already executes crossing orders atomically (Q lines 239–259), while P’s enforcement targets delayed chip obligations (P lines 196–203, 248–284); a one-trade side payment is only a change in effective price (ada #7). P’s own regular-trading result suggests the risk: natural-language vs structured contract has similar covered tiles but fewer trades (P lines 1381–1387), although transcript length and enforcement interpretation differ, so representation is not causally isolated. In Q, form buyer–seller plans under a fixed negotiation protocol, then randomize market runs after agreement to display verified identical terms in compact JSON vs concise prose; keep all execution in the original anonymous book and compare with no-plan and full-transcript arms. Measure realized surplus, crossing hazard, missed gains at \(T=300\), price dispersion \(\alpha\), and trade volume separately; test reliance after explicit plan expiry, not supposed knowledge of partner exit, because Q’s prompt hides identities (Q lines 621–635). Publication potential is a causal boundary test of whether negotiated language steers price discovery when commitment is already provided by the exchange. Unresolved: whether this effect exists, whether it replicates across models/market schedules, whether pre-round bilateral plans are a meaningful intervention in an anonymous market, and whether the exact design is novel after broader prior-work review (see #18).
